title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
gist: Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst describes how customer, safety and regulatory demands turned Digit 5 into a heavy (over 120 kg), forklift-like warehouse humanoid built for 20-hour duty cycles and safe coworking. He sees it as Agility's scaling moment, with RoboFab capacity above 10,000 units per year, while admitting it betrays his original vision of graceful motion.

insights.claim: Agility Robotics launched Digit 5, a humanoid warehouse worker built to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and run 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, aiming to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Humanoid vendors are shifting from demos to uptime and duty-cycle economics.
insights.quote: Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge

insights.claim: Digit 5 weighs over 120 kg and its battery and cooling take about 75 percent of the torso, with a dock delivering 240 amperes at 48 volts, and it can no longer run or jump.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Power and thermal engineering, not agility, dominate useful humanoid design today.
insights.quote: The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso

insights.claim: Hurst argues that a human-looking robot in a factory or warehouse today either can't lift the required weight or can't last a full shift, and if it's not covered with sensors it's likely unsafe to stand next to.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Skeptical filter for humanoid claims from competitors.
insights.quote: it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift

insights.claim: The RoboFab in Salem, Oregon has capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year, and Hurst calls Digit 5 the scaling inflection point for Agility.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Manufacturing capacity is in place ahead of demand proof.
insights.quote: The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.

insights.claim: Digit 5 is meant to work 20 hours a day, which no human can do, and to meet NIOSH lifting guidelines including repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching 1.75-meter shelves.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: The value proposition is utilization hours rather than human parity in dexterity.
insights.quote: Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do.

themes.theme: Safety and regulation as scaling barrier

insights.claim: Digit 4 deployments had to operate behind physical barriers separated from humans to satisfy insurance and regulators, which severely limited usefulness and made safe coworking a primary Digit 5 design goal that took two years.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Safety certification and insurance, not capability, gate humanoid deployment at scale.
insights.quote: the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands

insights.claim: Digit 5 uses certifiable sensing and, when a person approaches, sets down its payload, sits on the floor and cuts motor power before the person can touch it, which Hurst calls the only near-term verifiable approach though a slowdown for everyday robots.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Conservative stop-and-power-off safety limits throughput near people.
insights.quote: As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors

insights.claim: Commercial deployment required European CE compliance, North American UL certification and FCC electromagnetic limits, which felt tangential to the founder's dream but were absolute requirements.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Compliance costs are a moat and a cost for humanoid entrants.
insights.quote: European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits

insights.claim: Agility sold only 10 Cassie research bipeds at US $250,000 each, saturating that market, and the founders started without first identifying a customer problem.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Research-robot revenue was a dead end, forcing the pivot to product.
insights.quote: ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them

insights.claim: Bin handling was chosen as Digit's first job because it needs two arms to lift high and legs to move in narrow spaces, varies across sites so single-purpose automation hasn't covered it, and is constrained enough to be economically viable.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Beachhead selection logic for general-purpose robots: variable but bounded tasks.
insights.quote: Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

insights.claim: Early deployments consumed huge effort to keep operational, which arguably eliminated any profit, but kept the company learning and alive; Digit 4 became the world's first commercially deployed humanoid at GXO after Amazon testing.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Early commercial humanoid deployments are likely margin-negative learning exercises.
insights.quote: We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made.

insights.claim: Agility brought in a new executive team that forced Digit 4 EVT to add larger batteries and safety and compliance upgrades, after which the team mapped the first 10 use cases and designed Digit 5 from scratch.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Founder-led research vision gave way to customer-driven product management.
insights.quote: We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch

insights.claim: Hurst says Digit 5's roadmap extends beyond bins to item picking, machine tending, parts preparation and eventually assembly, with modular tool interfaces and as a data source for future behavior training.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Platform strategy depends on expanding task breadth after proving bin handling.
insights.quote: our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines

insights.claim: Hurst concludes that customer and product requirements 'revealed what my vision was missing' and expects commercial success to bring robots closer to graceful, human-level mastery of motion.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Commercial pull is positioned as the route to better robotics science.
insights.quote: Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing.
